# Oared war galley and ram tactics (`oared_galley_ram`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/military.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Warfare, security & deterrence (`military`)
- Deps: helped by copper_bronze
- Core idea: A long, light hull rowed by many men is independent of the wind and can ram or board. The trireme packs 170 oarsmen on three levels into a hull about 37 m long and drives a bronze-sheathed ram at the waterline of the enemy at 8 to 9 knots. Such ships are built light, hauled ashore almost nightly to dry out and to feed and water the crew, and cannot stay at sea in bad weather. Rome won at sea by turning sea fights into infantry fights with boarding bridges and grapnels.
- Pitfalls:
  - Galley slaves chained to benches are a film image; ancient rowers were mostly free paid citizens or allies, and convict rowers belong to the 16th–18th c.
  - Galleys carry water for only a few days and need friendly beaches, so sustained blockades depend on bases and provisioning
  - Ramming needs highly trained crews; an untrained fleet should board instead
  - The ram splits planking, it does not spear the ship; a rammed galley floats waterlogged rather than sinking
- History: greece: c. 700–650 BC – triremes at Corinth according to Thucydides (Phoenician priority possible); 480 BC – Salamis; rome: 260 BC – boarding bridge (corvus) at Mylae; 31 BC – Actium; 1st c. BC fleets mix heavy quinqueremes and light Liburnians; china: 2nd c. BC – Han tower ships (louchuan) for river and coastal war; 12th c. – Song paddle-wheel warships; islamic: 655 – Battle of the Masts, first major Arab fleet victory; 16th c. – Ottoman galley fleets; europe: c. 1500 – heavy guns mounted in the bows of galleys; 1571 – Lepanto, a major battle of Mediterranean galley fleets
- Read:
  - J. S. Morrison, J. F. Coates & N. B. Rankov, The Athenian Trireme (2nd ed. 2000)
  - Lionel Casson, Ships and Seamanship in the Ancient World (1971)
  - John F. Guilmartin, Gunpowder and Galleys (1974)
